latin.2562: CXXV. Itaque juxta illos, Efficacia gratiae consistit in certa congruitate, & contemperatione vocationis divinae cum libero arbitrio, qua posita, juxta praescientiam Dei sequitur infallibiliter effectus. Quae sunt verba Petri a Sancto Joseph capite septimo libri quarti, in Idea Theologiae speculativae, Resolutione 7. In tractatu vero de divina gratia observat congruitatem illam non esse sumendam simpliciter a loco, vel tempore; quasi gratia ideo sit efficax, quia datur loco & tempore congruo. Etsi enim certum sit, gratiam congruam & efficacem non nisi tempore congruo dari; ejus tamen congruitatem & efficaciam a tempore potissimum desumendam non esse; sed in vocatione ipsa assignandum aliquid, propter quod tali tempore & loco effectum est habitura: siquidem alia vocatio, etsi sufficiens, eodem illo tempore nihil proficeret. Ideoque ex ejus sensu, Congruitas illa gratiae nihil est aliud quam proportio quaedam, & accommodatio inter gratiam ipsam, & voluntatem sic affectam, ut infallibiliter sequatur operatio. Disput. 7. Sect. 9. num. 66.
latin.2563: CXXVI. Hoc autem sic explicat paragrapho sequenti. Deus, inquit, per scientiam suam infinitam, certissime novit quid unusquisque homo facturus sit, posito hoc aut illo rerum statu: An consensum daturus, necne; & quis modus vocationis idoneus, non tantum ut homo suadeatur, sed etiam ut persuadeatur: aliter enim constat moveri ambitiosum, aliter avarum, & sic de aliis. Ambitioso expedit proponere rerum humanarum inconstantiam, qua multi ex summo honorum culmine repente dejecti sunt. Avaro vitae brevitatem, & incertam mortis horam, &c. Et quia inter ambitiosos diversa sunt ingenia, item inter avaros; uni proponenda sunt exempla, alii rationes ex Philosophia, vel Theologia desumptae, alii similitudines ex rebus notioribus captae; ut ita unus isto, alius alio modo ad poenitentiam inducatur. Imo vero unus & idem homo diversis diebus, horis, ac momentis alius est a seipso: Nunc ira, nunc gaudio, nunc tristitia afficitur; unde aliter hodie movendus & excitandus ac heri: & quae rationes efficaciter una hora suasissent, altera fortasse erunt inutiles: adeo verum est, quicquid recipitur ad modum recipientis recipi, nec omnia nobis eadem semper apparere, sed prout quisque affectus est, talem ei finem videri. Itaque homo interdum, tum propter circumstantias loci, aut temporis; tum propter varios passionum affectus, quibus agitatur, ita dispositus est, ut talis cogitatio seu illustratio intellectus, & talis affectus seu motio voluntatis sint illi debite accommodata, & contemperata ad conversionem illius perficiendam: quare in tali contemperatione auxilii & voluntatis sic dispositae, efficacia gratiae constituenda est.
latin.2564: CXXVII. Supponunt igitur authores istius sententiae Deum ab aeterno praescire per scientiam quam Scholae mediam, seu conditionatam vocant, quid hic aut ille homo facturus sit, si vocetur hoc aut illo modo, & si ad ipsum convertendum tales illustrationes & inspirationes, aliaque hujusmodi media, tum externa tum interna adhibeantur. Et quidem si hoc modo vocetur Petrus, verbi causa, illum secuturum, minime vero, si alio modo. Licet sive hoc sive illo modo vocetur, possit si velit sequi, vel non sequi.
latin.2565: CXXVIII. Deinde hoc posito dicunt Deum certos homines, exempli gratia, Tyrios & Sidonios decrevisse vocare & excitare ad conversionem, iis mediis & ea ratione, quae quidem potestatem eis revera dabant sese ad Deum convertendi si vellent, sed quae tamen certo praevidebat nullum apud ipsos effectum habitura; non vero iis mediis, quae si adhiberentur, praevidebat ipsos convertendos. Contra vero voluisse Ephesios, verbi gratia, vocare, non ea ratione quae ab ipsis respuenda esset, sed qua certo praesciebat ipsos ad fidem fore adducendos. Unde sequitur Deum decrevisse illis quidem dare gratiam, qua converti possent si vellent; at vero his gratiam qua actu converterentur.
latin.2566: CXXIX. Prior illa gratia est quam sufficientem vocant: posterior vero quam vocant efficacem. Qui priori modo vocantur, dicuntur vocari modo non congruo: Qui posteriori, modo congruo. Posterior haec vocatio originem habet a decreto, quo eorum qui vocantur conversio praedefinita est: prior vero non item. Et tamen gratia quae per priorem istam vocationem confertur, & sufficiens appellatur, juxta mentem istorum Doctorum, non distinguitur realiter, seu quoad entitatem Physicam, aut vim agendi, a gratia efficaci; sed tantum moraliter, seu per ordinem ad operationem secuturam: Licet enim quis non habeat auxilium efficax, quo de facto convertatur, potest tamen per illud quod dicitur sufficiens, actu converti si velit, sine novo auxilio, quod se habeat tanquam boni operis principium.
latin.2567: CXXX. Quanquam autem illi Theologi censeant auxilium quod dicitur efficax, non differre Physice & quoad entitatem realem, seu vim agendi, sed solum moraliter &, ut loquuntur, per ordinem ad secuturam operationem, ab eo quod solum sufficiens dicitur; nihilominus existimant illum qui efficaci auxilio donatur, longe majorem a Deo gratiam accipere, quam cui sufficiens duntaxat conceditur. Idque quoniam doni sive gratiae alicujus praestantia & magnitudo praecipue metienda est tum ex animo donantis, tum etiam ex utilitate & fructu qui redit ad accipientem. Jam autem auxilium efficax datur a Deo ex certo proposito hominem convertendi: sufficiens vero ad tale propositum referri non potest. Praeterea conversio quam operatur auxilium efficax, maximum est bonum quod inde redit ad eum cui Deus auxilium tale largitur. Auxilium vero sufficiens, quantumlibet in se magnum sit, cum tamen supponatur accommodatum & congruum non esse dispositioni illius qui accipit, ipsi manet prorsus inutile; quin per accidens ad majorem ejus damnationem cedit.
latin.2568: CXXXI. Itaque Doctores illi cum Molina dici nolunt ex duobus qui aequali gratia praeventi sunt contingere posse ut unus convertatur, alter non convertatur. Nam qui convertitur, semper majorem gratiam a Deo accepit, quam ille qui non convertitur. Supposita vero in pluribus omni ex parte aequali gratia, vel omnes convertentur, vel nullus convertetur. Ex eorum mente fieri quidem potest, ut in eo qui convertitur non sit, ex parte auxilii divini quo praevenitur, major mentis illustratio, & vehementior voluntatis motio, quam in eo qui non convertitur. Quin admittunt fieri posse ut in eo qui rebellis manet, mens spiritu divino luculentius illustretur, & voluntas fortius & vividius percellatur, quam in eo qui reipsa per gratiam efficacem ad conversionem & fidem adducitur. Sed in eo qui convertitur, qualiscunque divina motio, sive major sive minor, majoris gratiae semper, juxta ipsos, rationem habet, quoniam dispositioni illius qui recipit accommodata, & contemperata est; adeoque ex insigniori benevolentia Dei erga ipsum procedit, & cedit in majorem ejus utilitatem.
latin.2569: CXXXII. Sic docet Bellarminus, sententiam suam cum sententia Molinae & Lessii comparans, iis tamen non nominatis. Prima, inquit, opinio vult efficaciam gratiae pendere a voluntate humana, nostra vero pendere vult a voluntate Dei. Et, si proponatur quaestio, utrum si duo homines habeant eandem omnino gratiam excitantem & adjuvantem, saltem in actu primo, & eundem concionatorem audiant, & eadem signa videant: utrum, inquam, fieri possit, ut unus credat, alter non credat? Prima illa opinio respondebit, fieri posse: quia libera voluntas manet, & potest pro arbitrio gratiam sequi, vel ei resistere. At nostra sententia respondebit, posse quidem fieri, ut duo homines, eadem interna motione accepta, eundem concionatorem audiant, & eadem signa videant, & unus credat, alter non credat; tamen non posse fieri, ut si eandem omnino gratiam excitantem duo homines accipiant; unus credat, alter non credat. Siquidem ad gratiam non solum pertinet motio, sive excitatio interna, sed circumstantia loci, temporis, personae, &c. Si enim eadem motione accepta, unus credit, alter non credit, sine dubio unus accepit motionem eo modo, loco & tempore, quo Deus praevidit ejus ingenio congruere, alter non ita accepit; ac per hoc longe majorem habuit Dei gratiam, is qui credit, quam qui non credit. Qui enim non credidit, habuit gratiam qua posset si vellet credere; qui autem credidit, habuit gratiam qua posset & vellet credere. Tunc enim Deus in nobis operatur velle, quum ita vocat, ut videt secuturos. Et ideo vere non potest fidelis adversus infidelem gloriari, aut inflari: quia qui eum principaliter discernit ab infideli, non est ipse per liberum arbitrium, sed Deus per gratiam efficacem, quam ei dedit, alteri non dedit. De gratia & libero arbitrio lib. 1. c. 13. sub finem.
latin.2570: CXXXIII. Quibus similia tradit Petrus a Sancto Joseph in fine disputationis septimae tractatus de gratia divina. Auxilium divinum, inquit, duobus modis spectari potest, vel in genere entis, vel in genere beneficii. Si priori modo spectetur, fieri potest ut unus cum aequali, aut etiam cum majori auxilio non convertatur, & alter convertatur cum minori. Ratio est, quia cum gratia non determinet voluntatem, oblato duobus hominibus aequali auxilio in ratione entis, uterque manet indifferens ad consentiendum, aut non consentiendum. Quare unus illorum libere poterit consentire, etsi alter minime consentiat. Si vero auxilium spectetur sub ratione doni, & beneficii, tunc fieri non potest ut posito aequali auxilio, unus convertatur, non alter; quia auxilia tunc dicuntur aequalia in ratione beneficii, quando aeque prosunt: quare si unum ita prosit, ut reipsa effectum habeat, aliud minime, jam in genere beneficii aequalia non sunt.

sections.title: Efficacy as congruity of the call with free choice
sections.pass_a: CXXV. Therefore according to them, The efficacy of grace consists in a certain congruity, & attunement of the divine call with free choice, which being posited, according to the foreknowledge of God the effect follows infallibly. Which are the words of Peter of Saint Joseph in the seventh chapter of the fourth book, in the Idea of speculative Theology, Resolution 7. But in the treatise on divine grace he observes that that congruity is not to be taken simply from place, or time; as if grace were efficacious for this reason, because it is given at a congruous place & time. For although it is certain, that congruous & efficacious grace is not given except at a congruous time; yet its congruity & efficacy is not to be taken chiefly from the time; but something is to be assigned in the call itself, on account of which it will have effect at such a time & place: since another call, though sufficient, would avail nothing at that same time. And therefore in his sense, That congruity of grace is nothing else than a certain proportion, & adjustment between grace itself, & the will so affected, that the operation follows infallibly. Disput. 7. Sect. 9. num. 66.
pass_b: Thesis CXXV. On their view, then, 'the efficacy of grace consists in a certain congruity and attunement of the divine call with free choice; given this, the effect follows infallibly, in accordance with God's foreknowledge.' These are Peter of Saint Joseph's words in his Idea of speculative theology, book 4, chapter 7, resolution 7.

In the treatise on divine grace he notes that this congruity is not to be drawn merely from place or time, as though grace were efficacious just because it comes at a fitting place and time. Congruous and efficacious grace is certainly given only at a fitting time. Still, its congruity and efficacy are not mainly derived from the time; something must be found in the call itself that makes it take effect at that time and place, since a different call, though sufficient, would achieve nothing at that very moment. In his sense, therefore, 'that congruity of grace is simply a certain proportion and fit between grace itself and the will in such a state that the act follows infallibly' (disputation 7, section 9, number 66).

sections.title: God fits the call to each person's temper and moment
sections.pass_a: CXXVI. And this he explains thus in the following paragraph. God, he says, by his infinite knowledge, most certainly knows what each man will do, this or that state of things being posited: Whether he will give consent, or not; & what mode of calling is suitable, not only that the man be urged, but also that he be persuaded: for it is clear that the ambitious man is moved in one way, the avaricious in another, & so of the rest. For the ambitious it helps to set forth the inconstancy of human things, by which many have suddenly been cast down from the highest summit of honours. For the avaricious the shortness of life, & the uncertain hour of death, &c. And because among the ambitious there are diverse temperaments, likewise among the avaricious; to one examples are to be set forth, to another reasons taken from Philosophy, or Theology, to another likenesses taken from better known things; so that thus one in this, another in another way is led to repentance. Nay indeed one & the same man on different days, hours, and moments is other than himself: Now he is affected by anger, now by joy, now by sadness; whence he must be moved & roused otherwise today than yesterday: & the reasons which would have persuaded efficaciously in one hour, in another will perhaps be useless: so true is it, that whatever is received is received according to the mode of the receiver, nor do all things always appear the same to us, but as each one is affected, such does the end seem to him. Therefore man sometimes, both on account of the circumstances of place, or time; and on account of the various affections of the passions, by which he is driven, is so disposed, that such a thought or illumination of the intellect, & such an affection or motion of the will are duly adjusted to him, & attuned to accomplishing his conversion: wherefore in such an attunement of the aid & of the will so disposed, the efficacy of grace is to be placed.
pass_b: Thesis CXXVI. He explains this in the next paragraph: 'Through his infinite knowledge God knows with complete certainty what each person would do in this or that state of affairs: whether he would consent or not, and what manner of calling would be suitable for him not merely to be urged but to be won over. Plainly the ambitious man is moved one way and the greedy man another, and so with the rest. To the ambitious it is useful to point out how unstable human affairs are, since many have been suddenly thrown down from the very height of honour; to the greedy, the shortness of life and the uncertain hour of death, and so on. And because temperaments differ among the ambitious, and likewise among the greedy, some must be shown examples, others reasons drawn from philosophy or theology, others comparisons taken from more familiar things, so that each is brought to repentance by his own route.

Indeed one and the same person differs from himself from day to day, from hour to hour, from moment to moment. Now anger grips him, now joy, now sorrow; so today he must be moved and stirred in another way than yesterday, and reasons that would have persuaded him effectively in one hour may prove useless in the next. So true is it that whatever is received is received in the manner of the one receiving it, and that things do not always look the same to us; the end appears to each of us according to how we are disposed. At times, then, because of circumstances of place or time and because of the various passions that stir him, a person is so disposed that a given thought or illumination of the mind, and a given affection or motion of the will, are duly fitted to him and attuned to bringing about his conversion. The efficacy of grace must therefore be located in this attunement between the aid and the will so disposed.'

sections.title: The supposition: God's middle knowledge
sections.pass_a: CXXVII. The authors of this opinion therefore suppose that God foreknows from eternity by the knowledge which the Schools call middle, or conditional, what this or that man will do, if he be called in this or that way, & if for converting him such illuminations & inspirations, and other means of this kind, both external and internal be applied. And indeed that if Peter, for example, be called in this way, he will follow, but not at all, if in another way. Although whether he be called in this or in that way, he can if he will follow, or not follow.
pass_b: Thesis CXXVII. The authors of this view therefore assume that God foreknows from eternity, by what the Schools call middle or conditional knowledge, what this or that person would do if he were called in one way or another, and if such illuminations and inspirations and other means, outward and inward, were used to convert him. If Peter, say, is called in this way, God knows he will follow; if in that way, not at all. Yet whichever way he is called, he can follow or not follow, as he wills.

sections.title: Tyre and Sidon called incongruously, Ephesus congruously
sections.pass_a: CXXVIII. Next, this being posited, they say that God decreed to call & rouse certain men, for example, the Tyrians & Sidonians, to conversion, by those means & in that manner, which indeed truly gave them power to convert themselves to God if they willed, but which nevertheless he foresaw for certain would have no effect with them; but not by those means, by which if they were applied, he foresaw they would be converted. But on the contrary he willed to call the Ephesians, for example, not in that manner which would be rejected by them, but in that by which he foreknew for certain they would be brought to faith. Whence it follows that God decreed to give to the former indeed grace, by which they could be converted if they willed; but to the latter grace by which they would actually be converted.
pass_b: Thesis CXXVIII. On that basis they say that God decreed to call and stir certain people to conversion, the Tyrians and Sidonians for example, by means and in a manner that did truly give them power to turn to God if they wished, but that he foresaw with certainty would have no effect on them. He did not call them by the means he foresaw would convert them if used.

The Ephesians, by contrast, he willed to call not in a manner they would reject, but in the one by which he foreknew for certain they would be led to faith. It follows that God decreed to give the first a grace by which they could be converted if they wished, and the second a grace by which they would in fact be converted.

sections.title: Sufficient and efficacious differ only morally
sections.pass_a: CXXIX. That former grace is what they call sufficient: the latter what they call efficacious. Those who are called in the former way, are said to be called in a non-congruous way: Those in the latter, in a congruous way. This latter calling has its origin from a decree, by which the conversion of those who are called is predefined: but the former not so. And yet the grace which is conferred through that former calling, & is called sufficient, according to the mind of these Doctors, is not distinguished really, or as to Physical entity, or power of acting, from efficacious grace; but only morally, or by order to the operation that will follow: For though one have not the efficacious aid, by which he is in fact converted, he can nevertheless through that which is called sufficient, actually be converted if he will, without a new aid, which stands as the principle of the good work.
pass_b: Thesis CXXIX. The first grace is the one they call sufficient, the second the one they call efficacious. Those called in the first way are said to be called incongruously; those called in the second, congruously. The second calling originates in a decree by which the conversion of those called has been predefined; the first does not.

Even so, on these doctors' view, the grace conferred through the first calling and named sufficient is not really distinct from efficacious grace, whether in physical entity or in power to act. It differs only morally, that is, in its relation to the act that is to follow. A person may lack the efficacious aid by which he is in fact converted, yet through the aid called sufficient he can actually be converted if he wishes, with no new aid serving as the source of the good work.

sections.title: Yet the one given efficacious aid receives far greater grace
sections.pass_a: CXXX. But although those Theologians think that the aid which is called efficacious, does not differ Physically & as to real entity, or power of acting, but only morally &, as they speak, by order to the operation that will follow, from that which is called only sufficient; nevertheless they think that he who is endowed with efficacious aid, receives far greater grace from God, than he to whom sufficient only is granted. And this because the excellence & greatness of any gift or grace is chiefly to be measured both from the mind of the giver, and also from the usefulness & fruit which returns to the receiver. But now efficacious aid is given by God from a certain purpose of converting the man: but sufficient cannot be referred to such a purpose. Further the conversion which efficacious aid works, is the greatest good which returns from it to him on whom God bestows such aid. But sufficient aid, however great it be in itself, since it is supposed not to be adjusted & congruous to the disposition of him who receives it, remains wholly useless to him; nay by accident it turns to his greater damnation.
pass_b: Thesis CXXX. These theologians hold that the aid called efficacious does not differ from the aid called merely sufficient physically, in real entity or power to act, but only morally, or as they put it, in relation to the act to follow. Even so, they consider that whoever is given efficacious aid receives a far greater grace from God than one granted sufficient aid alone. This is because the worth and size of a gift or grace are to be measured chiefly by the intention of the giver and by the benefit and fruit that come to the receiver.

Efficacious aid is given by God with a settled purpose of converting the person; sufficient aid cannot be traced to any such purpose. Moreover, the conversion that efficacious aid brings about is the greatest good its recipient gains from it. Sufficient aid, however great in itself, is assumed not to suit or fit the disposition of the one who receives it, so it stays entirely useless to him; indeed, incidentally, it turns to his greater condemnation.

sections.title: Against Molina: equal grace, unequal outcome is impossible
sections.pass_a: CXXXI. Therefore those Doctors will not have it said with Molina that of two who have been prevented by equal grace it can happen that one is converted, the other not converted. For he who is converted, has always received greater grace from God, than he who is not converted. But equal grace in every respect being supposed in several, either all will be converted, or none will be converted. In their mind it can indeed happen, that in him who is converted there is not, on the side of the divine aid by which he is prevented, a greater illumination of the mind, & a more vehement motion of the will, than in him who is not converted. Nay they admit it can happen that in him who remains rebellious, the mind is more clearly illuminated by the divine spirit, & the will more strongly & more vividly struck, than in him who is in fact brought through efficacious grace to conversion & faith. But in him who is converted, whatever the divine motion, whether greater or less, has always, according to them, the character of greater grace, since it is adjusted, & attuned to the disposition of him who receives it; and so it proceeds from a more signal benevolence of God toward him, & turns to his greater advantage.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXI. These doctors therefore refuse to say with Molina that of two people forestalled by equal grace, one may be converted and the other not. Whoever is converted has always received more grace from God than the one who is not. Granted grace equal in every respect among several people, either all will be converted or none will.

In their opinion it may well be that, as regards the divine aid that goes before him, the convert has no brighter illumination of mind and no stronger motion of the will than the one who is not converted. They even allow that the mind of someone who stays rebellious may be lit more clearly by the divine Spirit, and his will struck more forcefully and keenly, than in someone actually brought to conversion and faith by efficacious grace. Yet in the convert the divine motion, whether greater or smaller, always counts on their view as greater grace, because it is suited and attuned to the disposition of the one receiving it. It thus springs from a more striking goodwill of God toward him and works to his greater benefit.

sections.title: Bellarmine: equal inward motion, unequal grace
sections.pass_a: CXXXII. So teaches Bellarmine, comparing his opinion with the opinion of Molina & Lessius, these however not being named. The first, he says, opinion will have the efficacy of grace depend on the human will, but ours will have it depend on the will of God. And, if the question be put, whether if two men have entirely the same exciting & assisting grace, at least in first act, & hear the same preacher, & see the same signs: whether, I say, it can happen, that one believes, the other does not believe? That first opinion will answer, that it can happen: because the will remains free, & can at its pleasure follow grace, or resist it. But our opinion will answer, that it can indeed happen, that two men, having received the same inward motion, hear the same preacher, & see the same signs, & one believe, the other not believe; but it cannot happen, that if two men receive entirely the same exciting grace; one believe, the other not believe. For to grace belongs not only the motion, or inward excitation, but the circumstance of place, time, person, &c. For if, the same motion being received, one believes, the other does not believe, without doubt the one received the motion in that way, place & time, in which God foresaw it would be congruous to his temper, the other did not so receive it; and by this he who believes had far greater grace of God, than he who does not believe. For he who did not believe, had grace by which he could believe if he willed; but he who believed, had grace by which he could & would believe. For then God works in us to will, when he so calls, as he sees they will follow. And therefore the believer truly cannot glory, or be puffed up against the unbeliever: because he who chiefly distinguishes him from the unbeliever, is not himself through free choice, but God through efficacious grace, which he gave to him, did not give to the other. On grace & free choice book 1. c. 13. toward the end.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXII. This is Bellarmine's teaching, comparing his own view with that of Molina and Lessius, though without naming them. 'The first view,' he says, 'makes the efficacy of grace depend on the human will; ours makes it depend on the will of God. Suppose the question is put: if two people have entirely the same exciting and assisting grace, at least in first act, hear the same preacher and see the same signs, can it happen that one believes and the other does not? The first view will answer that it can, since the will remains free and can follow grace or resist it at its own choice.

Our view will answer that it can indeed happen that two people receive the same inward motion, hear the same preacher, see the same signs, and that one believes while the other does not. But it cannot happen that two people receive entirely the same exciting grace and one believes while the other does not. Grace includes not only the inward motion or stirring but also the circumstances of place, time, person and so on. If the same motion is received and one believes while the other does not, then beyond doubt the one received it in the manner, place and time that God foresaw would suit his temperament, and the other did not; and so the believer had a far greater grace of God than the unbeliever.

The one who did not believe had grace by which he could believe if he would; the one who believed had grace by which he could and would believe. For God works the willing in us when he calls people in such a way as he sees they will follow. So the believer truly has no ground to boast or swell with pride over the unbeliever, since what chiefly sets him apart from the unbeliever is not he himself by free choice but God by the efficacious grace he gave him and did not give the other' (On grace and free choice, book 1, chapter 13, near the end).

sections.title: Peter of Saint Joseph: aid as being and as benefit
sections.pass_a: CXXXIII. Things like these Peter of Saint Joseph teaches at the end of the seventh disputation of the treatise on divine grace. The divine aid, he says, can be regarded in two ways, either in the genus of being, or in the genus of benefit. If it be regarded in the former way, it can happen that one is not converted with equal, or even with greater aid, & another is converted with less. The reason is, because since grace does not determine the will, equal aid in the character of being being offered to two men, each remains indifferent to consenting, or not consenting. Wherefore one of them will be able freely to consent, though the other in no way consents. But if the aid be regarded under the character of gift, & benefit, then it cannot happen that equal aid being posited, one is converted, not the other; because aids are then called equal in the character of benefit, when they profit equally: wherefore if one so profits, that it in fact has effect, the other not at all, they are already not equal in the genus of benefit.
pass_b: Thesis CXXXIII. Peter of Saint Joseph teaches much the same at the end of the seventh disputation of his treatise on divine grace. 'Divine aid,' he says, 'can be viewed in two ways: as a being or as a benefit. Viewed the first way, it can happen that one person is not converted with equal or even greater aid while another is converted with less. The reason is that grace does not determine the will; when equal aid, considered as a being, is offered to two people, each stays undetermined between consenting and not consenting, so one of them may freely consent though the other does not consent at all.

But if the aid is viewed as a gift and benefit, it cannot happen that, given equal aid, one is converted and the other not. For aids are called equal in the order of benefit when they benefit equally; so if one aid benefits to the point of actually taking effect and the other not at all, they are already unequal in the order of benefit.'
